chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Idris (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: My father narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Alawi. He said: Ahmad ibn al-Qasim narrated to me from Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari. He said:

I was afflicted with extreme poverty, so I visited Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both) and he permitted me in. When I sat down, he said: O Abu Hashim! Which of the blessings of God the Mighty and Majestic upon you would you like to give thanks for? Abu Hashim said: I was struck dumb, not knowing what to say to him.

So he (AS) preceded and said: He has given you faith, by which He has forbidden your body from the Fire. He has given you wellness, by which He has supported you in obedience. And He has granted you contentment, by which He has preserved you from self-abasement.

O Abu Hashim! I only addressed you first with this because I thought that you wanted to complain to me about the One who has done this to you. And I have ordered one hundred gold coins for you — so take them.

key_terms.الإيمان: faith (iman) — belief that protects from Hellfire
key_terms.التبذل: self-abasement, degradation through excessive need or begging
key_terms.عز وجل: Mighty and Majestic — an epithet of God
key_terms.مائة دينار: one hundred gold dinars — a substantial sum
key_terms.نعم الله: the blessings of God — a Quranic concept (cf. 14:34)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali al-Hadi say to Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari about God's blessings when he came in poverty?
ai.summary: Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari, a close companion of the Imams, visited Imam Ali al-Hadi (AS) in a state of extreme poverty, intending to seek financial help. Before he could speak, the Imam preempted him by enumerating three foundational divine blessings — faith, health, and contentment — framing them as gifts far greater than material wealth. This account is set in the context of the Abbasid period (mid-3rd century AH) when Shia scholars like Abu Hashim often faced economic hardship. The Imam then mercifully also provided one hundred dinars, demonstrating that spiritual wisdom and material generosity are not mutually exclusive in the Imami tradition.
